title: What makes an act good (CCC 1750–1756)
hookLine: the act itself, the intention and the circumstances

lines: SAME ACT FROM THE BACK PEW.
cards: Sunday, the collection basket comes down the pew. Three envelopes go in. The first is from a woman who heard the parish is helping a family that lost its home in a fire.
The second is from a man who folds his so the person beside him can see how thick it is. The third is from a woman who lost her job last month and gave anyway, less than she used to.
From the back of the church, all three look identical. What makes an act good?

teach.b: The Catechism answers with three things, which it calls the sources of morality. First, the object: what is actually chosen. Giving money, telling the truth, telling a lie.
Reason looks here first, and some acts are wrong whatever the reason behind them.
Second, the intention: why, the end a person has in view. One intention can run through a whole string of actions, and one action can carry several intentions.
Third, the circumstances: who, where, when, how much, under what pressure. Then how they fit, and the Catechism is plain. A good intention can't make a bad act good.
Its example is lying: even to help a neighbor, a lie is still a lie. In one short phrase: the end does not justify the means. It goes the other way too: a bad intention can spoil a good act.
The example comes from Jesus, about giving alms to be seen. In the Douay-Rheims: "sound not a trumpet before thee." The man folding his envelope for the pew is doing a good thing for a hollow reason.
Circumstances can make an act more or less good, more or less serious; fear, for instance, can lessen a person's responsibility. But they can't turn a wrong act into a right one.
So a good act needs all three together: a good object, a good intention, fitting circumstances.

teach.h: THE END DOES NOT JUSTIFY THE MEANS.
teach.b: And the third envelope? Thinner, maybe. But a lost job and a tight month add weight to that gift.

how: Catholic moral teaching weighs an act by its object, its intention and its circumstances, and some Catholics use those three in an examination of conscience before confession.

games.q: what does “what makes an act good” mean?
o: a good act, a good reason and fitting circumstances
an act that turns out well for most people
any act done with good intentions behind it

games.q: the three sources — tap the pairs.
p: can raise or lower the weight
a good act spoiled by display

s: a good intention can make any act good
the Catechism says a good intention can't make a bad act good: the end does not justify the means.
a bad intention can spoil a good act
the Catechism's example is giving alms in order to be seen.
circumstances can turn a wrong act into a right one
they can lessen or increase goodness and responsibility, but can't make a wrong act right.

games.q: a coworker made a mistake and asks you to tell the boss a small lie to cover it. your reason is kind: you want to protect her job. what does the Catechism say about that lie?
o: the kind reason makes the lie good.
the lie is still wrong, even with a kind reason.
games.why: the Catechism uses lying as its example: a good intention doesn't make a bad act good. the end does not justify the means.

practice: Bring up one decision in front of you this week: a message to send, money to spend, a favor to say yes or no to.
Name the what plainly, then the why, honestly, even if it's a little embarrassing, then the when and how: who's affected, the timing, the pressure.
Notice which of the three is the shaky one, and if you pray, ask for light on that one.

wordCard.voice: What makes an act good. The Catechism names three sources: the act chosen, the intention, and the circumstances, and asks that all three be good together. Today's word.
